Luo constructed a subsequence of square-root-dense lattice points within hyperbolic Pythagorean triangles, which are associated with non-primitive Dirichlet characters, in a manner that mirrors the arrangement of points suggested by Michel and Venkatesh. Building on this framework, our research introduces a concept of quantum unique ergodicity for Hecke-Maass newforms in relation to Dirichlet characters and demonstrates its widespread occurrence by utilizing the autoregressive properties of Selberg's eigenforms, Harvey's theorem on character Dirichlet L-function zeros, and the Jutila-Luo formula for character Hecke series. Moreover, our findings regarding quantum unique ergodicity hold when considering Landau-Siegel roots of Hecke-Maass newforms.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare framework from <12, 13> to expect that programs will prevent undesirable outcomes from happening, rather than guaranteeing a particular result. This modified framework, which we call the "quantum relational separation" or QRS framework for short, includes a rule for assigning meaning to the guarantee that a program will prevent some undesirable effect from occurring, as well as a proof rule that allows us to reason about the prevention of undesirable outcomes from happening. This rule is essentially the same as the rule for guarantees in the quantum relational Hoare framework. Furthermore, we have discovered that the predicate transformation function associated with the prevention of undesirable outcomes can be seen as a form of backward reachable states with respect to the transition relation defined by the program, which has significant implications for the relationship between predicate transformations and the behavior of programs in the quantum setting.

The rapid transmission of contagious diseases in crowded areas, coupled with limited vaccination rates in certain populations, pose significant threats to global health. Mathematical models, which account for varying contact rates over time and include a small number of super-spreader occurrences, can effectively simulate the spread of diseases in crowded settings. This paper focuses on examining existing models and presents two new, integrated models, one with constant and one with time-dependent contact rates. A team of researchers found that one of these new models aligns with the existing model showcasing Seoul virus transmission in Korea.

Codiskcyclicity in collections of operators on topological vector spaces is a well-defined concept that has been extensively studied in the literature.
In the context of the article, codiskcyclicity is reinterpreted as a crucial property that ensures the existence of a specific type of invariant.
The main goal of the paper is to provide an in-depth exploration of codiskcyclicity in collections of operators on intricate topological vector spaces by utilizing an alternative, equivalent definition that the authors believe is more suitable for this particular setting.
The article also introduces the concept of a codiskcyclic collection of operators that is invariant under a given group action and uses it to develop codiskcyclicity testing theorems.
The authors further demonstrate the applicability of these theorems through specific examples related to the symmetries of Euclidean spaces and also provide a codiskcyclicity testing theorem for collections of operators on the space of square matrices.

Accurate measurements of solar vector magnetometry are crucial for in-depth studies of magnetic field properties and magnetohydrodynamic phenomena on the Sun. Researchers have developed and refined post-processing inversion algorithms to retrieve magnetometric information from spectrographic data, with various implementations showing mixed results in validation tests. A key issue with these algorithms is the risk of introducing circularity bias when using synthetic magnetographic images to calculate the azimuth angle of magnetic fields, despite efforts to validate them through forward modeling. This study analyzes the underlying causes and consequences of this bias and explores methods for identifying and lessening its effects, ultimately contributing to the development of a new inversion algorithm that minimizes circularity bias in magnetometric measurements for solar applications.

A type of neural network, complex-valued multilayer perceptron, can simulate neural interactions analogous to Fermi systems, which may help in addressing the sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo methods. We used a non-contour-integral version of this model to train on complex-valued data representing fermionic operators and checked that the optimization yields accurate results without running into the Hubbard sign dilemma. We found that complex-valued learning enables the correct classification of distinct fermionic modes without facing the dilemma, and this effect persists even when noise is introduced. By employing a specific complex-valued optimizer, we successfully solved a model meant to mimic fermions with double occupancy, which has been a major challenge due to the sign dilemma.

Given a subshift in the standard topological context, we investigate how its topological entropy and symbolic complexity respond when it undergos a series of mappings defined by a monoid action and basis changes defined by a free group base. We provide specific formulas for the resulting entropy and complexity in these scenarios. We discuss the presssing issue of whether there exist analogs of the Sharkovsky ordering for hypersystems defined by a free group base.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-based method known as Reverse Dense Retrieval (RDR), which selectively incorporates relevant examples from a vast dataset to refine the model's performance.
RDR exploits both positively identified instances and contrasting negatives to adapt the model, differentiating it from existing dense retrieval methods that solely utilize positive examples.
Our proposed approach, which employs RDR in conjunction with dense retrieval for a hybrid model, demonstrates superior performance in unsupervised settings, according to our experiments conducted on datasets like the Cross Formulation Language (CFL) and human-written text.
These results indicate that our method is effective in expediting the transition between linguistically similar tasks without requiring explicit guidance, in addition to surpassing baseline models in evaluation metrics like the mean average precision.

In the context of sensitive data, such as medical images, that is shared across platforms for AI training and application, regulatory compliance demands both privacy and security. While privacy-focused algorithms like differential privacy address these issues, they introduce unnecessary complexity for many purposes. We contend that a well-optimized standard model typically meets functional and security requirements. To support this claim, we refined a robust neural network model and employed a Bayesian optimization method to minimize loss function for a hypothetical competing model, ensuring our model's superiority. Furthermore, we validated our findings against artificial data sets, demonstrating the generality of our findings.

The concept of a boolean structure is a natural extension of boolean algebra to groups that can be defined as containing no elements besides the identity, except for those conjugate to a specific generating set of size three, whose conjugate pairs form a non-cyclic subgroup of order six. These structures have three distinguishing features: they incorporate the properties of a symmetric group, a holomorph of the symmetric group S6, and the automorphisms of the non-cyclic part of a specific finite field F₆₉. We establish that within the group G₆₉ of order 51840, which is characterized by having maximal simplicity and only prime power orders for its elements, there exists a subgroup that is isomorphic to the symmetric group S6 and has a maximal embedding in G₆₉, thereby meeting the criteria for a boolean structure.

Researchers employed a two-step method to analyze chemical data from 67,700 stars in the APOGEE-2 database, focusing on five elements (Mg, Al, Si, P, and Cl) that are sensitive to mixing occurring during the formation and evolution of the solar system. By removing redundant indicators, they developed a two-procedure approach to model the observations, separating core processes affecting elemental ratios. This model highlighted various populations of disks associated with stars of different masses and ages, as well as two primary planetary material ingredients: a primitive, metal-rich component and a processed, metal-poor one. This model also highlighted the significance of oxygen in defining these populations and revealed a relationship between planetary material and the solar system's inner temperature. Notably, this analysis discovered a previously unknown population of disks with high levels of phosphorus and chlorine, likely resulting from the interaction between solar system materials and a planetary body that occurred in the early stages of the solar system's formation. This finding has implications for our understanding of planetary chemistry and the behavior of solid elements in the solar system's core.

In 2020, China experienced a significant spread of rumor information related to COVID-19 on its social media platforms. To combat this issue, the Chinese government launched a specialized rumor-refutation campaign, utilizing influential online figures to create and disseminate counter-narratives. This study investigates the effectiveness of this campaign and the factors influencing the dissemination of rumor information. It also explores how the spreading of rumor information affects individuals' behavioral changes and psychological responses. A survey of 1,500 participants in China, in conjunction with a computational modeling of rumor spread using the SIR model, provides the methodological basis for this research. The findings reveal that the influential online figures' refutations can suppress the spreading of rumors and accelerate the recovery of affected individuals in local communities. Moreover, the Chinese government's swift response in limiting the physical spread of COVID-19 has significantly reduced the transmission of rumor information in China. The research also discovers that the widespread of rumor information can lead to increased anxiety levels among individuals in local communities and accelerates the transmission of rumor information in urban areas. The underlying mechanisms of this phenomenon are attributed to the diverse social networks in urban areas and the influential online figures' tendency to follow popular information on COVID-19 in these settings.

A new catalog of 1166 PN in 18 early-type galaxies in the Fornax cluster becomes the largest catalog of PN in this cluster to date, with a median distance of 5.75 kpc from galaxy centers. This catalog, created using a semi-automated method, incorporates data from the $H\alpha$ and [N\,\textsc{ii}] bands from the VLT/MUSE survey and is complete for PN with a luminosity of log($L_{\rm PN}/L_\sun) \geq 3.65$. A significant finding is that the PN distances can be reliably determined through a data-driven machine learning approach ignoring external information about the galaxies, and this method performs significantly better than a traditional, galaxy-specific approach for all but the two most distant galaxies in the sample. This catalog also contributes to the study of galaxy assembly by providing a detailed analysis of PN within specific mass ranges and offers a potential tool for investigating the structure and mass profiles of early-type galaxies through the study of PN kinematics and dynamics.

Thanks to continuous advancements in sensor technologies and rising costs for data storage, stream processing has become increasingly prevalent. While existing stream processing engines can handle massive amounts of data for one-time events, they struggle with regular streams that follow established patterns. These streams repeat previous data through periodic cycles, reinventing unnecessary costs for data processing and storage. In response to this challenge, this paper introduces LifeFlow, a stream processing engine optimized for cyclic streams. LifeFlow identifies repeating patterns in data streams and creates persistent representations that underpin efficient operations. By leveraging this approach, LifeFlow significantly reduces overhead for data storage and processing, outperforming leading stream processing engines like Apache Flink and Apache Storm by up to 92 times in testing scenarios.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined and its characteristics identified for curves in six-dimensional Euclidean space.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a critical decision with far-reaching implications for both training and subsequent operational use. Loss functions serve as the foundation for several prominent variants, including Crammer's multi-class loss functions and the hatched loss function for class imbalance problems. The success of these variants is closely tied to their underlying loss function components. Despite the significance of loss functions in neural network development, the existing literature is characterized by a limited understanding of the theoretical underpinnings and the existing research mainly focuses on presenting and evaluating empirical results without delving into the underlying analytical framework. In contrast to a prevailing "try it and see" approach, research on multi-class loss functions, such as Crammer's and the hatched loss function, can be analyzed through a lens of performance prediction and metric analysis, offering a more in-depth examination of loss function influence, as well as a more precise performance prediction framework, which can be utilized to forecast the impact of performance assessment loss function alteration on these specific loss functions.

This research utilizes a combined experimental and numerical approach to investigate the microstructural changes caused by strain-induced crystallization in polyethylene films under various temperatures and tensile loads. The accompanying mechanical and morphological transformations were studied using infrared thermal imaging, optical microscopy, and atomic force microscopy. A reduced representation of the material's behavior was replicated using a thermomechanical simulation, accounting for the interplay between chemical and mechanical processes, and was validated through comparison with the observed results. The simulation was subsequently employed to investigate potential future experiments and revealed that decreasing the drawing rate or introducing nucleating agents could significantly impact the microstructure's development.

To analyze the magnetism in an anisotropic $s$-wave superconductor with broken rotational symmetry, we used a quasi-one-dimensional model and found strong evidence for a type of spin-density wave instability that can coexist with the superconducting state. This state exhibits anisotropic behavior, similar to that found in an $d$-wave superconductor. A key characteristic is the occurrence of a positive magnetic susceptibility for small enough external fields. This susceptibility is enhanced as the external field is aligned with the superconducting order parameter's angular momentum. A notable finding is that the positive susceptibility can persist even when the spin-density wave becomes the dominant ground state, forcing the superconducting state to change to an $d$-wave type. This change is induced by the competition between the external pressure and strain. A Ginzburg-Landau theoretical approach supports these results and provides a quantitative analysis of the susceptibility's enhancement.

Continuous phase modulation detection without coherence has a disadvantage in combatting delay-induced symbol errors, making it less desirable for channel estimation in comparison to coherent detection. It is demonstrated in this paper that for certain conventional n-coherent differential CPM detection systems, a well-suited delayed replica can be found to enhance the detection method's resistance to errors caused by time shifts, eliminating the need for coherent detection. A comprehensive analysis of these systems through simulations and theoretical error rate analysis for $m$-ary differential phase shift keying and $m$-ary differential amplitude phase shift keying is provided, along with delayed replica selection guidelines.

Building upon the concept of quantum gravity introduced in a prior work, where the metric tensor is treated as a quantum variable within the Johansen-Jannus, Mottola, and Cooperman (JMC) approach, the potential for gravity is redefined in its negative form to prevent singularities. This revised potential serves as a source of energy density for Einstein's gravity equation. The modified equation yields a non-singular Big Bang model and suggests that the gravitational field may exhibit compressibility at very low energies. The proposed model also offers an alternative to the Hubble tension and provides the opportunity for further investigation into the matter density parameter.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday factual statements inferred from conditional relationships, which are readily accepted as true by the majority of AI models without a need for further verification.  We contend that this type of knowledge is fundamental to AI intelligence and has not been previously addressed in existing knowledge bases.  In response to this gap, we present a comprehensive atlas of this kind of knowledge, comprising over 150,000 detailed descriptions of everyday situations together with corresponding conditional explanations for them.  This atlas is specifically designed to facilitate rigorous assessment of various AI models as well as the development of more sophisticated inference systems capable of processing complex conditional logic.

The field of finance relies heavily on calculating complex expectations via options on underlying assets. Researchers can utilize finance instruments like options to mitigate investment risks. Quantifying these expectations involves solving a scalar version of the HHL algorithm, which can be efficiently solved using a variational version of HHL. This paper presents an optimized implementation of the variational HHL algorithm, specifically tailored for finance applications and compliance with gate-based quantum computers. When tested on a real quantum processor, the paper shows that this variant of the algorithm can provide reliable asset allocation recommendations by accurately estimating option payoffs and assessing associated risk levels. The research also compares the proposed method to a standard HHL implementation using classical simulation tools and verifies that the predicted performance holds true. The associated risk assessment and asset allocation models demonstrated in the study can be represented using classical simulated data and may serve as benchmarks for future quantum finance applications. The associated risk assessment and asset allocation models demonstrated in the study can be represented using classical simulated data and may serve as benchmarks for future quantum finance applications.

To improve the performance of our previously proposed multimodal speech recognition model, we have developed a dual-focused approach where both the text and image encoders have the ability to take the lead in training. This allows for the exchange of information between the encoders and the decoders, enabling the model to make use of both the ordered sequence of characters from the transcription and the disordered set of characters derived from the speech waveform. By utilizing both of these inputs, the encoders are able to jointly learn a representation that combines both streams of information. This results in a more sophisticated learning representation that enhances the performance of our original model, as shown in the experimental results.

This research examines the concept of parking functions, a well-known idea introduced by Stanley in 1980. We generate a uniform distribution of parking functions for each natural number n, denoted as PF_n, and determine the characteristics of their initial positions asymptotically. Our primary goals are to identify the expected maximum value, the sum of the initial positions, and the number of distinct first positions as n approaches infinity. Our primary discoveries include using combinatorial methods to establish precise formulas for these characteristics and demonstrating that as n grows infinitely large, the expected maximum value, the sum of the initial positions, and the number of distinct first positions all approach (n+1)^2.

Measurements of quantum conductance in superconducting nanowires are influenced by the state of nearby charge control electrodes and vary based on the electrode's history. We observed that, below a certain threshold, the conductance exhibits periodic variations as it moves through the change in magnetic field, which corresponds to the change in charge state. This behavior can be compared to previous findings on niobium nitride nanowires and offers a contrasting result, with implications for the theories that attempt to explain these phenomena, including the idea of coherent quantum phase-jumps and Coulomb obstruction.

In highly dynamic environments like sports, predicting the future based on visual information is a critical skill, and one that can significantly influence decision-making on the field. However, research in visual prediction and related areas has largely ignored consideration of a competitor's perspective. To bridge this gap, a novel approach is presented that simultaneously predicts multiple possible futures from a single present moment, incorporating a competitor's perspective. This approach, which utilizes a dual representation to connect different viewpoints, enables the model to generate multiple future perspectives without specifying their likelihood. To evaluate this method, a dataset with multiple possible futures was created, but conventional evaluation metrics are found to be less effective due to their reliance on a single best forecast. Therefore, a new evaluation strategy is devised that accounts for the diversity of possible futures, their spatial coherence, and their alignment with ground truth labels. Using this framework, the proposed approach is compared to a baseline method, demonstrating its superiority. Next, the algorithm is applied to a challenging video forecasting task in American Football, where the future is predicted from various viewpoints, and the best forecast is selected based on future game states. This approach offers a suitable platform for expanding the model to multiple viewpoints without difficulty.

In a recent study, the one-electron states of a $3d$ metal atom, nickel, were empirically ascertained within a $TiO_2$ lattice, and the autoconsistency of its computational method was validated. Nickel's $d$-band shape resembles that of a freely moving electron, and the tiny energy differences between its one-electron states are comparable to those reported in theoretical studies, demonstrating the practical application of their developed approach.

The AMR collaboration has recently observed $\Omega^{-}$ baryons with three strange quarks in $p$-wave states through ALICE at the LHC and ABC at the BNL, following the proton-proton and lead-proton collisions. Although $\Omega^{-}$ baryons are well-studied, especially in their ground states, there is a lack of research on their excited orbital angular momentum states, particularly focusing on the $1^3D_3$ state with minimal knowledge regarding its spectral structure. Thus, our work aims to thoroughly investigate the $\Omega^{-}$ baryon's $1^3D_3$ state by utilizing quark models that account for both the internal and external movements of quarks. By applying the Spectral Gennesbach method and considering the influence of the Melosh transformation, we generate a detailed spectrum of $\Omega^{-}$ baryons and compare our results to empirical data and theoretical predictions derived from QCD. Our research indicates that the $1^3D_3$ state's spin-orbit splittings can be either positive or negative, depending on the quark correlative force's intensity, and that it shares similarities with the $1^3D_3$ state of the $\phi$ meson. Moreover, our findings align with earlier predictions made by Ioffe and his colleagues.

Understanding how to prevent the spread of infectious diseases in crowded areas, where transmission risk is high, is crucial for public health policy-making. This study examines the value of a well-mixed framework for modeling transmission in closed systems, specifically using the example of urban bus transportation. By comparing a simple compartment model to a super-sp spread model, we assess the implications of using a well-mixed model for predicting transmission and mortality rates in buses. Our results indicate that a well-mixed model overestimates transmission and mortality rates by a factor of two. This research provides quantitative insights to inform modeling choices and offers a way to estimate the impact of interventions, such as air purification and mask-wearing, on reducing transmission and mortality in crowded settings.

The spin accumulation and decay in a Bi/Co multilayer system have been investigated through theoretical modeling, considering the impact of spin-orbit interaction and interface roughness. The study demonstrates that the magnitude of spin accumulation near the interface depends on whether the interface is sharp or rough, and that the accumulation becomes more significant in the coating layer when the interface is smooth. The research also reveals the influence of the spin-orbit interaction on the drift length of spins, showing that it is minimal compared to the rough interface's effect. The predicted outcomes are the exhibition of the Anisotropic Magnetoresistive (AMR) and the Spin-Orbit Torque (SOT) switching phenomena in the coating Bi layer. The theoretical framework can be applied to other material combinations exhibiting strong spin-orbit interaction.

This paper provides a higher dimensional generalization of the fractional Schrödinger equation for a specific type of potential, allowing time invariance and confirming that the time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation yields solutions to this potential when considering the Jumarie type of fractional derivative in both its standard and modified forms.

We introduce a novel neural network regularization technique called enforced Lipschitz consistency, which complements the existing method of training neural networks to meet the Lipschitz continuity requirement. We contend that strictly adhering to defined boundary conditions is essential in ensuring our neural networks satisfy the desired Lipschitz continuity properties. A key innovation of our technique involves incorporating an additional layer to predict a set of pseudo-inputs, which are then utilized to assess the Lipschitz continuity of neural networks through the calculation of their Lipschitz continuity errors. We have conducted an extensive series of experiments which demonstrate our technique to be highly effective in neural networks trained for the tasks of image classification and manipulation. Our findings show that enforcing a minimal level of Lipschitz continuity results in significant improvements in their performance, while adhering to tighter constraints yields outcomes on par with, and in some cases surpassing, those obtained with data augmentation and truncated vascular regularization, which are considered established benchmarks in the field.

We have performed a comprehensive analysis of inclusive Drell-Yan vector boson production, specifically focusing on W and Z bosons, within the context of third-generation gauge vector leptoquark theories. This study takes into account the interplay between these vector leptoquarks and third-generation fermions and delves into the possible implications for their masses. Our investigation was conducted utilizing the CutTools and O'Mega libraries to compute higher-order corrections and implement the calculation within the Sherpa event generator. Our results for massless and massive case corrections are presented and compared with existing literature. Furthermore, we have derived constraints on vector leptoquark masses by analyzing three major datasets and have explored the predicted outcomes for leptoquark pair production and W/Z boson pair production with additional heavy fermions.

Traditional artificial neural networks (ANNs) may not perform well with low-dose PET images, which have a lower signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) than regular dose images, due to limited training data and different statistical properties. To improve the effectiveness of ANNs in such scenarios, we propose a novel method that incorporates a physics-based prior in the form of a Gaussian process (GP) to enhance the robustness of the network to noise and low-dose images. This GP prior serves as both a feature enhancer and a source of regularization, enabling the network to adapt to a wide range of SNRs, including those outside of its training distribution. We further introduce a robust training technique called uncertainty-aware knowledge distillation (UAKD) to enhance the network's performance. In UAKD, the training and knowledge transferring processes are treated as inverse problems that are solved using the GP prior and data similarity. We validate our approach using real low-dose PET images and find that it significantly outperforms the conventional network in terms of image quality and segmentation accuracy, with a 30% reduction in dose required to achieve the same performance as a high-dose reference group.

A key principle of centering theory, which underpins coreference resolution, posits that in each utterance, there's a prominent entity, often previously mentioned, to which the current sentence is linked. While this theory has been embedded in coreference models, the benefits of this integration are unclear. Our investigation into modern neural coreference models, using the GUM corpus as our test subject, reveals they already achieve high performance comparable to trained machine learning models, without relying on centering principles. By disabling the incorporation of centering features, we found these models to be inherently resistant to violations of defined centering conditions. In situations where the predicted antecedent violates established conditions, models trained on general language data can select an alternative antecedent 57% of the time, and with 10% lower cost than models trained on centering-annotated data. Our analysis suggests that these models' ability to capture the inherent structure of language has led to the automatic incorporation of basic centering properties, allowing them to efficiently navigate complex linguistic scenarios.

Wireless communication systems are prone to varying levels of signal loss due to different environmental obstructions in real-world settings. In Bluetooth and low-energy Bluetooth scenarios, assessing the communication range is a complex task that can be both time-consuming and costly, with results showing that signal strength correlates poorly with range, depending on the specific scenario. To overcome these challenges, researchers have been exploring machine learning models to predict range dimensions, with studies indicating that such approaches can yield accurate results with minimal data. In contrast, most research has focused on WiFi signal prediction rather than range assessment. To bridge this gap, the project employs a dataset from a previous study, combining feature sets from a Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) and WiFi signal strengths, before utilizing a subset of these features in a trained model to predict rectangular area dimensions. The evaluation shows that, when using a limited number of features, the model can accurately forecast area sizes, with an average error of just 3 square meters.

The beam beam interaction can lead to beam loss in energy recovery linacs and is exacerbated by beam planks losing coherence due to transverse oscillations. The degree of coherence is determined by the rate of beam loss and is affected by the strength of the beam beam interaction, as well as the energy spread of the beam. A theoretical model is presented that accounts for filling pattern dependent effects on beam loss coherence, and demonstrates a significant impact of beam loss coherence on beam stability, particularly in large beam filling scenarios. The model also highlights the complexity of beam instability, particularly beam planks at the end of a ring that experience beam beam interaction twice, once with a beam plank of the same species moving in the opposite direction, and again with a energy displaced beam plank moving in the same direction. The model indicates that these planks experience strong drive bunch instability inside their respective cavities, and are significantly more unstable than any other beam planks within the ring.

Building upon the fundamental one-loop three-glone vertex function, specifically the central-emission part, we derive the one-loop two-glone two-photon vertex function in N=4 SYM theory. The former can be expressed in terms of the two-glone two-photon vertex function through a Lorentz-invariant overlap integral, essentially a convolution. This convolution maintains the vertex function's vertex property and ensures the two-glone two-photon vertex function satisfies the conservation of momentum. We further provide the explicit mathematical representation of the two-glone two-photon vertex function in both Lorentz covariant tensor form and as a series of Lorentz scalar products. We also offer a Lorentz-covariant derivation of the two-glone two-photon vertex function by directly applying a specific set of gauge-invariant Ward identities. This approach yields identically the same results obtained through the convolution method. We conclude by examining the implications of these findings for two-glone scattering amplitude calculations in N=4 SYM theory.

Research has shown that extremely elongated polymer bristles under high forces have a specific pattern of stretching, where the longest dimension is typically greater than ten times the thickness, and these dimensions are proportionally consistent across various shapes and forms of bristles, from curved and branched structures to thin films, unless they are near a surface or in a narrow confining space, in which case the stretching ratio can significantly differ, even by as much as half, and these reduced ratios can vary greatly based on the bristle's form, surface interaction, and how much it is stretched, rather than any specific thickness or dimension, and these reduced ratios have been labeled as "end exclusion regions" that all polymer bristles enter at some level of stretching, in which they cannot stretch to a certain fraction beyond a certain thickness, even with immense forces applied.

A set of positions in a metric space is said to have the classic version of dimension d if it's possible to pinpoint d distinct points within the space using their distance vectors. A graph's dimension is then defined as the minimum dimension of which its vertex set can be represented. We introduce a new concept, half-dimension, which requires a smaller number of positions to identify half the distinct points in the space. We establish key properties of half-dimension and demonstrate its relationship to the embedding of a complete binary tree in a graph. Notably, a graph has a large minimum degree and lacks a perfect matching if and only if its half-dimension equals its dimension, and in this case, we find an upper and lower bound for its half-dimension of two and infinity respectively.

Researchers used a machine learning approach to analyze all-sky maps generated by the Fermi-LAT satellite, specifically in the energy band between 1 and 3 GeV, where the instrument faces significant background limitations. The machine learning algorithm, specifically an adaptive boosting variant, was utilized to categorize sources based on their constant or variable emission patterns. The method was tested on mock data and then applied to actual data for 1068 sources listed in the third Fermi LAT catalog. The study showed that the majority of sources with high confidence levels (greater than 3 sigma) exhibit variable emission patterns, with the majority falling within the 1-10 year timescale for changes in their radiation intensity. A subset of 34 sources with the most variable emission patterns was also identified, and further analysis indicated that many of these sources exhibit radiation pattern changes within the 1-10 year timescale for timescales as short as 1 year in certain energy bands. A notable finding involves the blazar source M87, which the study determined changed significantly over a 50 day period in 2015, with a timescale that precedes the detection of its giant flare on March 27, 2017.

In a sequence of two-person dictatorships, where a dictator makes a decision for two individuals with different preferences, various rules can be applied to the last dictator. A rule that evaluates the outcome of the sequence in comparison to a given reference outcome is defined as a comparative standard. We examine two categories of comparative standards: those that prioritize consistency and those that prioritize responsiveness. We discuss how standards that promote responsiveness can result in sequences of decisions that are more desirable than a serial dictatorship system based on a specific criterion, but may prioritize the preferences of the last dictator over those of the first, leading to undesirable outcomes in some cases. In contrast, standards that prioritize consistency can guarantee that the system is better than a serial dictatorship in specific scenarios. We also compare our analysis to previous research and offer a potential improvement.

We present a method for detecting binary asteroids using images from the Pan-STARRS1 telescope, which we apply to a large dataset of 83,415 near-Earth asteroids without orbital characteristics. By analyzing the distribution of detected objects within each image, we developed a statistical approach to identify pairs of closely spaced objects that represent binary asteroids rather than optical artifacts caused by the telescope. Factors influencing our detection accuracy include the separation of the pair, the brightness of the individual components, and the image's noise level. A detection model, supported by metadata on the telescope's operations and image preprocessing, helps us account for these variables and prioritize valid binary asteroid detections. The most likely pairs meeting our criteria have a semi-major axis of one Earth radius or less, a period of less than three days, and a light curve amplitude of ten percent or more. However, many potential binary asteroids remain undetected in our sample, suggesting that future observations with higher sensitivity, such as those from ZTF and LSST, may reveal many more binary asteroids with wider orbits and lower light curve amplitudes.

In recent years, the partial linear model has been widely applied across various fields, incorporating machine learning components to capture complex relationships. This work extends the partial linear model to include multiple endogenous variables and provides efficient estimation methods, building on the instrumental variables regression and the empirical process of continuous sampling. A theorem for asymptotic normality is proven for the model's parameter of interest, as well as a theorem for a consistent estimator for the model's average treatment effect. A simulation study is conducted to compare the performance of different estimation methods, and a real-world application involving peer influences in a educational network is presented.

This study extends Leibniz's general rule to both basic and classical Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integral and derivative operators. Key extensions are achieved by applying these rules to various functions, including constant, exponential, logarithmic, power, Bernoulli, Euler, Abelian, and Eulerian functions. Furthermore, the rules are substantiated through computations involving the operators and derivatives of these functions.

We've developed a system to guide players through text-based adventure games using natural language guidance, taking into account their previous actions and decisions. This approach was effective in leading unfamiliar players through a simple dungeon and a more complex one from the Sword Coast Adventurers' Guide, while also successfully recreating famous Dungeons and Dragons scenarios. Our method has been surpassed by a more advanced model, but we believe our starting point could be a useful foundation for similar endeavors.

Proteins that are naturally occurring in their knotted form pose a complex problem for structural biology researchers, as their three-dimensional arrangement doesn't fit with the standard rules of protein assembly. A recent study categorized the native, knotted proteins that make up a significant portion of a particular genetic dataset and identified several common patterns, particularly with regard to how these proteins bend and curve. By examining these patterns, the study demonstrates a novel approach to pinpointing the possible routes these proteins could take as they bend, based solely on their existing knotted three-dimensional structure, without referencing any comparison data. This method, which uses topological information and geometry, was applied to a subset of protein data known as topologically complex proteins and shows that their simple, curved shapes hide more intricate configurations that could be revealed by looking at their three-dimensional structure in a different light.

Let $\omega$ be a symplectic form on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ or $\mathbb{S}^{2n}$, and consider the category $\mathcal{R}_c(\omega)$ that consists of symplectic mappings with compact domain and without boundary. A key characteristic of this category is the absence of a well-defined notion of genus. To address this, we introduce an alternative parameter, $r$, which represents the number of blowup points in the domain. This results in the creation of a family of monoid groups, parameterized by $r$, that we term the strong rational mapping category groups associated with $\omega$ and denoted as $\Pi_{sr}(\omega)$ or simply $\Pi_{sr}$ when $\omega$ is implicit. Notably, when $\omega$ corresponds to the standard form on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$, these groups exhibit isomorphic characteristics to those of the monoid groups associated with odd integers, whereas on $\mathbb{S}^{2n}$, they exhibit isomorphic characteristics to those of the monoid groups associated with non-negative integers.

The Irrelevance Theorem has been applied to the NG boson in symmetric phase in both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theories, indicating that the NG mode from an arbitrary U(1) symmetry can be made massless, albeit coupled strongly to other modes of the system, such as a Debye photon in the nonrelativistic example. However, this statement does not hold for the NG mode resulting from a broken translation symmetry, as seen in the example of the one-dimensional, discrete version of the Hubbard model, where the theorem's failure leads to the formation of a soliton/olmerock that is inherently massive and localized within the lattice, despite being NG in character.

Recent advancements in counterfactual language models have focused largely on individual-level modifications, whereas the potential for phrasal-level changes has gone underutilized. Our proposed project aims to explore the capabilities of large language models in creating counterfactual language that involves multiple word changes, particularly in the context of question-answer pairs. We have created a dataset called DISCO, which comprises question-answer pairs with designated counterfactual modifications, leveraging platforms like Wikipedia and Quora. Our findings indicate that large language models like T0 can effectively generate counterfactual language for single-word changes, but they struggle with multiple-word alterations. Furthermore, we discovered that these models often prioritize preserving the original semantic meaning of a question over generating plausible answers in its modified form. Our future plans for this project involve developing methods to address the observed limitations and evaluating the potential uses of counterfactual language in applications like training more robust models and manipulating language for educational purposes.

We investigate the epitaxial growth of MnGa Heusler layers on a graphene/sapphire surface using in situ X-ray scattering techniques during molecular beam epitaxy. This process is highly sensitive to the preparation of the graphene substrate and the deposition parameters. We observe three distinct epitaxial growth modes: van der Waals epitaxy near the substrate edge, long-range epitaxy through a "supernucleation" effect induced by a pinhole in the graphene layer, and step-flow growth along graphene-induced steps on sapphire. This diversity of epitaxial growth modes offers opportunities for designing and tailoring materials properties through epitaxial constraints and strain-induced effects.

A recent study introduces a novel class of error-correcting codes called $\Z_p\Z_{p^2}$-linear codes, which can correct errors resulting from byte transmissions in applications like wireless communication networks. These codes have two key parameters: the rank k and the minimum distance d. A specific method is established to determine the dimension k of these codes, and an in-depth analysis is performed on a particular class of $\Z_4$-linear codes to illustrate this concept. Moreover, an alternative definition of the dimension k is provided and its relationship to the dimension of a related matrix is examined. A key aspect of these codes is that they possess a well-defined generator matrix, enabling the use of standard decoding techniques. A subsequent study on $\Z_p\Z_{p^2}$-linear codes examines their decoding capability and performance in comparison to other error-correcting codes.

In real-world applications, labels frequently take the form of text, dates,
images, or other data types rather than binary vectors. Although there have
been significant advances in multi-label learning, the majority of research
uses categorical response variables, which are composed of binary indicator
variables. This study introduces a novel problem where labels are in the
form of individual data points rather than binary vectors, and we call it
MLIP (Multi-Label Instance Problems). The problem is then formulated as a
supervised learning task where each sample belongs to one of the N labels,
which are defined as specific data points. A suitable approach for this
problem is proposed by drawing on the strengths of both encoding categorical
variables and using positive examples. The proposed method involves selecting
a subset of the N labels as positive examples and encoding the remaining labels
as binary variables. This results in a regularized binary multi-classification
problem that can be solved using off-the-shelf optimization tools. The
proposed method is compared to competing methods using experiments on real-world
datasets, and it outperforms these baselines in terms of classification accuracy
and model size.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated Hilbert spaces. This construction has various applications across quantum physics and quantum information theory. A key aspect is the relationship it maintains with the fundamental principles of physical postulates, including the requirement for positivity of matrix elements. This positivity is critical for ensuring reliable predictions from the theory. The positivity can be expressed in terms of a specific cone within the space of Hermitian operators, also known as the 'positive semi-definite cone'. The relationship between the algebras of physical observables, configurations, states, and the semi-definite cone suggests a abstract abstract biequivalence. A similar connection exists for certain types of non-commutative spaces defined by specific types of operator algebras. Building on the work of Landrie-Channe, Rennie, and Wock Birth, we introduce a new abstract biequivalence that encompasses both of these relationships and use it to derive the GNS construction as well as the Haag-Kastler and local quantum field theory, quadratic constraints, implementations of physical principles.

The mystery surrounding the origin of very high energy gamma-rays observed in nearby galaxies that emit significant amounts of radio waves needs to be solved. Two possible explanations for this phenomenon have been proposed - extremely collimated cosmic rays impacting the disk and high-energy photons being produced when magnetic fields in the disk force gas to move rapidly, before this gas is consumed by the galaxy's supermassive black hole. Although extremely collinated cosmic rays can account for gamma-rays in some galaxies, our research suggests it can only do so for a small subset of the well-studied galaxies, AGN-IGMs. In contrast, gamma-rays can be explained by the rapid acceleration of gas in all of these galaxies, and we estimate that the energy required for this process would be comparable to the energy released when the gas is eventually consumed by the black hole.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods could be more effective with automated tools.  M-mode echocardiography produces high-quality heart sound recordings that can help in this early detection, but they come in scanned forms that can be affected by various factors such as the echocardiogram device used, scan speed, and wall thickness.  These factors cause scanned recordings to differ significantly from each other, making them harder to distinguish with traditional machine learning methods.  To address this issue, a new method was developed that can effectively learn the patterns of these scanned recordings and compare them more accurately.  The proposed technique demonstrated a 6% improvement in accuracy over existing methods in distinguishing normal and abnormal heart sounds in scanned recordings made from various echocardiogram devices.  Additionally, the method showed promising results in differentiating between heart sound categories based on data from different scan speeds and wall thicknesses.

In the context of escalating healthcare data privacy concerns and stringent regulations, developing accurate machine learning models without violating data confidentiality has become increasingly essential. This concern is particularly significant for wearable healthcare devices that continuously generate real-time health data and require simple, portable models for health risk classification. Our research addresses this challenge by introducing FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare. FedHealth enables the seamless integration of multiple federated models, allowing for the efficient sharing of knowledge and statistical correlations across datasets. This innovative framework can be applied to diverse healthcare scenarios, including heart disease prediction in this study. FedHealth's effectiveness is demonstrated through comparative evaluations, revealing substantial improvements in model performance when compared to standard federated learning approaches.

This study provides a mathematical framework for optimizing portfolio performance by utilizing higher-order central moments, including skewness and kurtosis, in a multi-asset context. A key aspect of our approach is utilizing equilateral moments to ensure positive asset weights, which are otherwise constrained in traditional optimization methods. Our methodology offers flexible options to suit different return assumptions and allows for the incorporation of market impact and credit risk components. A thorough numerical example and real-world data set illustrate the method's applicability and highlight the effects of varying return assumptions and asset weights on performance measures.

The rise of automated system administration and the growth of software collections necessitate automated handling of software. This paper introduces AHRD, the Automated Handbook for Rough Configuration, a tool designed to streamline the installation and management of open-source software in university computer clusters and similar settings. AHRD automates software configuration, resolves dependencies, and tackles tough installation issues by leveraging existing installation guides and advanced string manipulation techniques. This work presents a novel approach to tackling software installation challenges and provides a practical solution for managing large software repositories.

This research focuses on a dynamic hedging problem where the cost component is subject to sudden jumps, and it identifies both upper and lower bounds for the minimum hedging cost among all possible strategies that can toggle the market's volatility in response to price movements, taking into account the incidence of transaction costs and market interruptions. Moreover, we establish that, under specific conditions, the most cost-effective strategies that respond to price changes by toggling the volatility, resulting in flat value processes, can be achieved through a variety of means, including but not limited to, the utilization of predictable toggling sequences, eventual quenching, or the application of a dual representation with an adjustment process that isgrally convex.

Initially, researchers only considered even leptoquark production pairs without accounting for the possibility of odd pairs, which could also form. We are modifying the existing framework to investigate both even and odd leptoquark duo creation. By utilizing the existing even pair production framework for reference purposes, we are comparing it to the new odd pair production of leptoquarks that can be created from collisions between protons. Even production pairs that the collider can detect through specific subatomic particles, such as electrons and neutrinos, require that the protons that collide have a similar energy level. In contrast, the energy levels of the colliding protons that can create uneven leptoquark pairs are not as rigidly defined and can result in differing energy levels of the produced leptoquarks, even in individual collisions. Even leptoquark duo creation that the collider can detect is primarily associated with a particular subatomic particle called the gluon. We analyze the role of external intergalactic radiation in heating and stimulating molecular gas in galaxies through the submillimeter C I lines, by using a model for intergalactic radiation and gas physics simulations. These lines, being less affected by optical depth than CO, allow for the determination of actual and stimulated temperatures in the molecular gas. This is particularly useful in studying gas in low-mass galaxies, as their molecular components are often optically thin and resistant to star formation suppression. By considering the unique properties of C I, we find that external radiation can account for a significant portion of line brightness in gas with high column densities in massive galaxies, but its impact is more pronounced in low-mass galaxies. This effect is more noticeable in the [3P2]-[2P1] line, as it is more easily stimulated than in the [3P2]-[2P2] line. This could have implications for understanding the relationship between gas and star formation at the galactic and cosmological scales.

In 2018, a research challenge was issued to solve the series reconstruction problem for permutations using the Hamming distance. This problem involves analyzing a sequence of partial permutations represented by their missing elements, with each permutation provided in the sequence being described by the positions that contain data. The objective is to reconstruct the original sequence of data values. This challenge has now been completed, and the corresponding solutions are being made available to the public for further comparison and analysis purposes.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Arrays (PTAs) will be sensitive to binary black hole mergers with low-frequency gravitational waves, especially those with orbital periods longer than half a day. Such binaries would primarily align with the plane of the PTA sky, causing their gravitational wave signal to repeat every one to several days that matches the Earth's motion relative to the source. This similarity in timescales leads to a large dataset required to synthesize PTA data, including hundreds of thousands of hours of raw data from individual telescopes, with hundreds of years of total observing time across all instruments. This challenge makes it difficult to utilize realistic, high-precision signal models for PTA data analysis, particularly when using cloud-based resources for matched filtering. A cost-effective solution to this problem would be to use simplified signal models, but this approach needs validation to ensure it accurately captures the key features of the signal detected by the PTA. Our study introduces an eccentric binary black hole sky map that can be used to visualize the characteristic gravitational wave signal of these sources, and it serves as a precise model suitable for PTA data analysis, even at the level of post-Newtonian parameters similar to those in GW150914. However, this model can be made less computationally expensive by reducing the precision of the signal model, and our analysis shows that this more affordable model still yields an accurate measurement of the binary's total mass, orbital frequency, and post-Newtonian parameters, even in datasets with a few

A key aspect of ASEP systems is the velocity function that measures the speed at which particles propagate. In this note, we outline the steps to derive specific velocity functions for ASEP, starting from general first-class conservation laws and utilising the compatibility of conserved quantities with the ASEP dynamics. We also examine the relationship between the velocity function and the matrix representation of conserved quantities, establishing a connection that can be used to determine the velocity function directly from the matrix representation. By applying and expanding on a prior study, we derive the velocity function associated with product measures, and demonstrate the utility of our method in extracting prior results.

Mathematical models have consistently been employed to analyze and manage the spread of infectious diseases throughout history, providing valuable insights for policymakers and public health officials, and offering a cost-effective means of exploring and evaluating different epidemic control strategies before putting them into practice. Historically, the most widely adopted models have been compartmental epidemic models, which categorize infected individuals into distinct epidemiological groups based on their transmissibility, and have been applied to analyze the spread of diseases in various settings, including both localized and globally interconnected populations. These models have been particularly useful in examining the impact of interventions such as lockdowns, as they can simulate the progression of an epidemic under multiple different scenario assumptions. Despite the availability of more sophisticated statistical models incorporating real-time data, compartmental models remain a trusted and reliable tool for assessing the outcomes of various control strategies and evaluating the efficacy of different epidemic mitigation tactics.

Researchers are focusing on the interaction between spinor atoms and particles like molecules, as they seek more comprehensive understanding and novel applications in the field of quantum simulation and metrology. The study of these interactions under specific conditions is challenging due to their fragile nature. This study introduces a method for studying the interaction between a particular kind of molecule and spinor atoms using particle-molecule collisions, inspired by a three-body recombination process induced by light. It shows that at low light intensities, a particular kind of molecule can be created through the interaction of two identical spinless atoms and a specific kind of particle, and that this process is controlled by a single parameter that determines the particle's state. It also demonstrates that at higher light intensities, a particle can be generated from the interaction of two identical spinless atoms and a particle with the opposite spin, a process known as three-body recombination, and that this process is likely used in the formation of molecule-pair condensates, a phenomenon that may be used for measuring the interaction between spinor atoms and particles.

The use of DNA storage is being considered for a wide range of applications, including data with complex hierarchy and persistent information requirements. Despite its potential, this technology has limitations, mainly due to constraints in sequencing technologies and reversible chemistry availability. To make the most of DNA storage, it's essential to maximize data storage efficiency and minimize the need for frequent hierarchy and information updates. This paper presents three key contributions aimed at addressing these challenges. Firstly, we introduce a novel hierarchy assistance method called "Self-Reference Encoding" (SRE), which enhances encoding efficiency and reduces hierarchy updates. Secondly, we develop a specialized DNA codeword conversion technique called "Codeword Shifting" (CS), designed to minimize codeword alterations. Thirdly, we design an optimized protocol for codeword conversions, including a two-phase approach called the "Codeword Conversion Hierarchy" (CCH), and an assessment of codeword change frequencies, both of which contribute to a reduction in codeword modifications. To evaluate our proposed solutions, we conducted a comprehensive simulation using a realistic DNA sequencing model, which showed our SRE hierarchy assistance method could lower hierarchy updates by 50% and codeword conversions by 70%, and our CCH protocol could decrease codeword alterations by 30% compared to existing methods.

An AI-powered solution for the shallow water equations is presented, allowing for efficient resolution for complex river flow problems. Traditional numerical methods, such as finite volume schemes, are combined with artificial neural networks to accelerate solving the equations, thereby optimizing computation time. A specific configuration utilizing a physics-informed neural network provides an alternative approach, both techniques resulting in solutions that closely mimic traditional methods when validated against established performance metrics.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels
to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. This research presents
a technique for automatically selecting and blending images for HDR photography
using a dual-exposure smartphone setup. A proposed algorithm determines the
optimal images based on a metric that prioritizes images with maximum detail
and minimal clouded areas. The technique involves employing image fusion to
counterbalance overexposed and underexposed regions. Experimentation among 20
participants and HDR-image-generation algorithms demonstrates that the proposed
method produces higher-quality HDR images. Furthermore, the technique is
efficient, utilizing approximately 10ms of processing power on a smartphone.

In this work, we outline a comprehensive framework for understanding how neural networks acquire causality, building on the concepts introduced in a prior work where we established a theory of neural network learning based on causality. The current framework is divided into three sections that explore the underlying principles of neural networks in relation to causality, the effects of data on network learning, and the impact of network learning on input signals. A comprehensive study is also presented to illustrate the key concepts and demonstrate the applicability of our framework across various network configurations and data types. Our findings reveal that our theory provides a precise explanation for established network phenomena and offers a novel understanding of newly observed patterns.

Given a map whose target is a closed manifold without a certain symmetry, a homotopy theory is used to analyze structured maps that can be made conformally consistent. A key principle, the b-principle, states that removing this target restriction is equivalent to adding the appropriate symmetry to the domain of the map. A specific case studies maps from a non-orientable surface to a surface with a high genus, examining how conformal symmetry affects these maps and whether it can be imposed on the domain.

The simulation of cardiac mechanics involves solving complex biomechanical problems with multiple moving boundaries, relying on the coupling of partial differential equations for mechanical and electrical processes, in addition to stochastic data for simulated arrhythmia models. Due to the problem's nonlinearity and the need to simulate various scenarios, realistic models require extensive computational resources, in excess of 100,000 cores, and prolonged simulation periods, exceeding several seconds for a single time step. In this research, multiple optimization strategies for multilevel preconditioning were comparatively evaluated to facilitate scalable simulations, with an emphasis on the effective distribution of computational tasks, efficient local solving, and optimal overlap between subdomains and solvers. A modern, high-performance computing infrastructure was leveraged to implement and test the analyzed methods, featuring up to 288 nodes, 9,600 cores, and an exascale-friendly parallel multiblock algebraic solver. Our studies yielded several key findings, including the beneficial impact of subdomain partitioning on performance, the limitations of direct solvers in dividing lines, the underutilization of available memory in some solvers, and the performance-enhancing effects of local resolving and robust algebraic subdomain solvers. Furthermore, we extracted actionable recommendations for research advancement in the field of cardiac mechanics simulations.

We employ a nonlinear integro-differential model to mimic the behavior of a diverse set of random permeability fields, which in turn influences the parabolic diffusion equation and leads to a fractional diffusion equation when properly averaged. The aim is to understand the random permeability's impact on a conservative transport equation, particularly in areas with diverse and complex terrain. The model accounts for the movement of substances in such environments by incorporating a fractional power law term that represents the desorption of substances from the soil. The associated mathematical proof includes establishing the solution's existence, uniqueness, and key properties, while also obtaining the solution to the corresponding backward problem and ultimately the random permeability's statistical properties from the averaged diffusion equation.

This study develops an analytical model to describe the interaction of light with optical resonators, waveguides, and other light sources, incorporating both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions. By utilizing a unified framework, we demonstrate how to determine the modes of these optical components and calculate the modes of a coupled system, including a light source and an optical component, for both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions. A generalized transfer matrix method is then introduced to examine the interaction of light with complex, multi-component systems, building on the individual mode calculations. This approach facilitates the calculation of eigenvalues, mode distribution, and phase space trajectories for a wide range of configurations, including both discrete spectra and mode locking, and provides a practical tool for designing mode-locked lasers and other optical devices.

In recent years, researchers have been concentrating on microfluidics. However, due to the small size of the tubes and the fast flow velocities, it is extremely difficult to conduct precise, high-resolution measurements of fluid flow within these tubes. As a result, there's a significant need for advanced imaging techniques that can restore high-resolution images from lower-resolution ones obtained through different imaging processes. Current image upscaling methods struggle to accurately restore images based on turbulent flow dynamics, especially when only a limited set of training data is available for modeling. In this paper, we introduce a new image restoration technique that utilizes both convolutional neural networks and generative adversarial networks to enhance the resolution of low-definition images related to fluid flow. When compared to existing methods, this technique demonstrates significant improvements in image restoration accuracy, especially when only a small sample of training data is available. In particular, our technique shows remarkable prowess in restoring high-resolution images from poorly defined ones obtained at a specific Reynolds number, as it can achieve a 45% increase in PSNR and a 25% boost in SSIM in our experimental settings. In our study on Reynolds numbers 200 and 600, we were able to restore high-resolution images from low-definition ones based on a limited set of training data, including a 3D model with geometric information, through the application of our technique that incorporates a novel position annotation feature. This resulted in images with incredibly precise flow dynamics, including detailed information about velocity, pressure, and three-dimensional flow

For large language models like BART, evaluating trained models on unsupervised tasks is a crucial step before applying them in real-world situations. Currently, available evaluation benchmarks are limited and don't account for model drift, posing a significant obstacle for model comparision studies. To address this challenge, we created L2Explorer, a cutting-edge evaluation ecosystem that incorporates numerous language understanding benchmarks and endless generated evaluation tasks through our Eternal Evaluation Framework. This ecosystem allows us to investigate endless evaluation scenarios, incorporate feedback from human assessors, and compare models through a variety of rigorous statistical tests. To facilitate accessible research, L2Explorer is designed with a user-friendly interface for both developers and researchers to effortlessly deploy new evaluation benchmarks, train models, and compare them using various metrics and analyses.

This thesis is comprised of two main sections. The first part focuses on the application of elimination theory to analyze and construct algebraic models for specific scenarios, including quadratic polynomials through Fano surface representations and certain types of plane curves configurations.
The second section of the thesis Concentrates on the geometric interpretation of a specific set of algebraic equations, ultimately aiming to demonstrate the integration of Descent Methods and Runge-Kutta techniques on a multi-parameter, multi-dimensional framework.

The relationship between galactic star formation rate (SFR) and molecular gas mass (M*) deviates from linear behavior for more massive systems, and this non-linearity is particularly pronounced in bulge-dominated galaxies. Utilizing a large data set containing high-resolution radio CO and far-infrared dust emission observations, we investigate the internal structure of massive galaxies and its impact on their SFR M* relationships. By separating CO emission into central and peripheral components, we identify three distinct populations of galaxies based on the contribution of their inner regions to their total SFR and M*. These populations reflect either gas-rich galaxies with low-mass bulges, gas-poor galaxies with high-mass bulges, and an intermediate group. Our analysis indicates that the gas held within the central regions of galaxies serves as a key driver in the non-linear SFR M* relationships observed, especially as gas in these areas is more compact and dense, thus more efficiently contributing to star formation. This, in turn, implies that the behavior of the SFR M* relationship can be re-expressed as a function of bulge mass, and this new formulation provides a more detailed understanding of the complex interplay between gas and star formation in massive galaxies.

This paper focuses on developing a sentiment analysis model that can be applied to multiple languages. A unique dataset is presented, consisting of three languages: English, Italian, and Portuguese, without any direct linguistic connection. A novel approach is proposed, utilizing a unified character set to create a way to analyze these languages charactoristically. The model's performance is evaluated in each language separately and also across their own character sets for the respective language pairs. A comparative analysis is conducted with a word-based model and our proposed character-based approach is found to achieve superior results. A interesting finding shows that training the model on a different language entirely can lead to improved performance in certain cases, a phenomenon known as multi-task knowledge gain, which is further investigated in separate experiments to define its parameters.

X-ray images hold significant potential for indicating whether a COVID-19 patient should be admitted to an intensive care unit.  Our proposed method involves creating a set of ICU admission characteristics from image features using machine learning and then selecting the most critical characteristics through genetic algorithm optimization.  To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, it was applied to a dataset of COVID-19 patients with mild, moderate, and severe symptoms.  By using a decision tree to derive key characteristics and image features, and a genetic algorithm to identify the most important characteristics, our results show that the proposed method can accurately predict the severity of patients with an average accuracy of 87.5%.  Furthermore, a genetic algorithm was utilized to identify the most significant characteristics, and our findings indicate that the top features include the presence of asymmetrical bilateral pneumonia, the pneumonia index, and the quantity of opacities in the lower lobes.  These findings are significant because they provide a starting point for developing a predictive model of ICU admission based solely on radiologic images of COVID-19 patients.
